curriculum.title: God Keeps His Promise to Sarah

core.big_idea: God kept His promise even after a long wait.

passages.reading_note: Read selected verses and focus on the promise, Sarah’s laughter, and God’s question.
Emphasise that the child was born at the time God had said.
Use with older children to recall that God had named Sarah and promised Isaac.

core.metanarrative_position: Covenant promise: God continues the promised family through Abraham and Sarah despite a long wait.

claims.statement: God promised that Sarah would have a son at the appointed time.
Sarah laughed because the promise seemed impossible in her circumstances.
Sarah gave birth to Isaac as God had promised and at the time God had said.
Isaac’s birth continues the covenant family through whom God would carry His promise forward.

core.interpretation_skill: Retell promise, waiting, fulfilment, and joy; do not turn one fulfilled promise into a guarantee about every request.

learning.foundation_objective: Retell that God promised Sarah a son, Sarah waited, and Isaac was born as God had said.
learning.extension_objective: Place Isaac in the promised-family story and explain that trusting God does not mean every wish is answered in the same way.
know: God made a specific promise to Abraham and Sarah.
Sarah found the promise hard to imagine.
Isaac was born as God had said.
understand: God is faithful even when waiting feels long.
A specific biblical promise must not be changed into a promise God did not make to us.
practise: Wait for one ordinary good thing without complaining.
Thank God for one promise He has kept in the biblical story.
become: A child who can wait, trust, and celebrate God’s faithfulness without demanding a timetable.
success_evidence: The child places Promise, Wait, Birth, and Joy in order.
The child says that God kept this specific promise.
The child names one patient action.

zero_prep_card.objective: Children retell the promise to Sarah and say that God kept it after a long wait.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: What is something small that is hard to wait for, such as a turn or a special day?
say: God had promised Abraham and Sarah a son.
The promise seemed impossible to Sarah, and she laughed.
God asked whether anything was too hard for Him.
Isaac was born at the time God had said, and Sarah rejoiced.
ask: What happened after the long wait?
What can patient trust look like this week?
zero_prep_card.do: Use the Promise and Waiting Path to place four events in order.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray: Faithful God, help us trust You and wait with patience.
materials: Promise and Waiting Path or four blank cards

preparation.passage_context: God’s promise of offspring has been repeated since Genesis 12. Genesis 18 announces an appointed time, and Genesis 21 records the birth of Isaac. The narrative is about a particular covenant promise, not a general promise that every desired child or outcome will be given.
text_observations: The visitors announce a specific time for Sarah to have a son.
Sarah laughs privately, and the Lord addresses the laughter directly.
Genesis 21 repeats that the Lord did as He had promised and at the time He had spoken.
interpretation_notes: Keep the lesson concrete: promise, waiting, fulfilment, joy.
Do not shame Sarah for finding the promise difficult; the narrative still records God’s faithfulness.
Use the name Isaac only as the child’s name; detailed wordplay about laughter is optional for older children.
theological_guardrails: Do not promise that God will give every family a baby or answer every request on the timetable they want.
Do not imply that infertility, pregnancy loss, or delayed answers are caused by weak faith.
Do not ask children to discuss private family fertility or loss experiences.

likely_questions.question: Why did Sarah have to wait so long?
likely_questions.purpose: Say that the passage does not explain every reason; it shows that God kept the promise despite the long wait.

likely_questions.question: Will God give me anything I wait for?
likely_questions.purpose: No. We trust the promises God has actually made and bring other hopes to Him without pretending He guaranteed the outcome.

discussion_questions.question: What exactly did God promise Sarah?
Why did the promise seem difficult to believe?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why difficulty does not change what God had promised.

discussion_questions.question: Which words in Genesis 21 show that God kept His word?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: The Lord did as He had said.

discussion_questions.question: What is one patient response we can practise?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Distinguish patient trust from pretending disappointment is not real.

activities.title: Promise and Waiting Path
steps: Add a waiting card with several footsteps.
Add the Isaac is born card.
Add the joy card and retell the story.
activities.learning_link: Makes a long narrative sequence concrete for young children.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Draw four boxes on a board and let children point.

activities.title: Patient Waiting Practice
steps: Let each child wait for a brief turn.
Connect ordinary waiting to patient character, not to earning a reward.
activities.learning_link: Practises patience without pretending it matches Sarah’s long wait.

closing.prayer_prompt: Thank God for His faithfulness and ask for patient trust.
closing.take_home_line: God kept His promise to Sarah even after a long wait.

family.title: A Promise Kept
family.parent_intro: This study uses a concrete story sequence to talk about waiting and God’s faithfulness.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Read Genesis 18:10-14 and 21:1-7, or retell the four events for a younger child.
Ask what God promised, what made it hard to imagine, and what happened at the appointed time.
Place four household objects in order for Promise, Wait, Birth, and Joy.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: Which words show that God kept His word?
How can we wait patiently for one ordinary thing this week?

interactive.title: Four-Part Promise Path
interactive.instructions: Use four objects as story markers and retell one sentence for each.

family.weekly_action: Choose one daily turn-taking moment and practise waiting without grabbing or complaining.
family.prayer: Faithful God, thank You for keeping Your word. Help us wait with patience and trust.
family.parent_note: Keep this lesson about the biblical promise. Do not connect it to private questions about pregnancy, babies, or loss.

quiz.question: Genesis 21 says the Lord did as He had promised.
Which action shows patience?
quiz.explanation: Patient trust can be practised in ordinary waiting.

puzzle.title: Promise, Wait, Joy
puzzle.instructions: Put the four events in order.

printables.title: Promise and Waiting Path
printables.purpose: Help children retell promise, waiting, fulfilment, and joy in order.

accessibility.reading_level: Short concrete sentences suitable for teacher-led reading with ages 4-8.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Use concrete verbs and define every abstract term through the story.
neurodiversity_supports: Allow pointing, drawing, or one-word responses.
Give one direction at a time.
sensory_notes: Participation must not require loud noise, touch, or public performance.
non_reader_support: Use pictures, objects, or gesture-supported retelling.

do_not_ask: Do not ask children whether their family wants, lost, or cannot have a baby.
Do not imply that a delayed answer proves weak faith.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Keep examples to ordinary waiting. Respond privately and follow pastoral or safeguarding procedures if a child independently discloses grief.
